title: Harvest home
hookLine: harvest festivals and Thanksgiving mark the end of the year's work
carry: they that sow in tears shall reap in joy

cards: The last wagon of sheaves comes up the lane toward the barn, and the field is finally bare. In English country tradition, that moment had a name: harvest home.
Tradition says a supper followed, for everyone who had worked the field, the farmer and the laborers at one table. The words made their way into hymns.
In the United States and Canada, a Thanksgiving table can still carry some of that feeling: a season's work done, and a meal to mark it. Today: harvest home.

teach.b: First, the song. An English hymn by Henry Alford puts today's word in its second line: "Come, ye thankful people, come, Raise the song of harvest home: All is safely gathered in, Ere the winter storms begin."
It celebrates not the profit but the relief: the work is done, and done in time. Second, the tears behind it. A psalm puts the harvest in a longer story.

teach.h: SOW IN TEARS, REAP IN JOY.
teach.b: In the King James words: "They that sow in tears shall reap in joy." Some of the sowing happened in bad years and worried seasons. The joy at harvest is the same field, seen from the other end.

Deuteronomy pictures a people settled in a good land and eating their fill, and says, in the King James words: "When thou hast eaten and art full, then thou shalt bless the LORD thy God for the good land which he hath given thee."

The next verses warn why: a full house is where forgetting starts. So the thanks is set at the moment of plenty, not only in the lean years. Jewish tradition takes this verse as the root of the blessing said after meals.
Fourth, your own field. You may never bring in wheat.
But a year of work has a harvest too: a project finished, a child grown a little, a skill that wasn't there before, a hard season gotten through. And some of it may have been sown in tears.
A harvest festival is a pause to look at what's gathered, call it by name, and give thanks, before the next season starts.

how: At harvest festivals, churches and communities decorate with produce, sing harvest hymns and share a meal, and the gifts are sometimes given away; Thanksgiving brings families together around a shared table.

games.q: the harvest is in, the barns are full, and you've just eaten well. by Deuteronomy, what comes next?
o: bless God for the good land.
games.why: "when thou hast eaten and art full, then thou shalt bless." the thanks comes at the full table, where forgetting is easiest.

practice: Look back over this year of your work, paid or unpaid, and let three things you've gathered come to mind: something finished, something learned, something survived.
If one was sown in tears, let that be part of it, and picture someone who helped you bring it in. If you pray, give thanks in your own tradition's words; if not, just say thank you.

wordCard.voice: Harvest home. The old name for the moment the last load is in, with a supper and thanks for the year's work. Today's word.
